column2: Then Subala's son, enraged, hurled at the Pandava a dreadful dart, like the Night of Time raised.
As it suddenly came, Sahadeva, laughing as it were, cut it in three in the battle with gold-adorned arrows.
It fell cut in three to the ground, gold-adorned, shattering like blazing lightning from the sky.
Seeing the dart destroyed and Subala's son afflicted by fear, all yours fled when fear arose, along with Subala's son.
Then a great shout was raised by the victorious Pandavas, and all Dhritarashtra's men then mostly turned away.
Seeing them dejected, the glorious son of Madri held them back in the battle with many thousands of arrows.
Then Sahadeva approached Subala's son as he went, guarded by Gandharas on horseback, holding to victory.
Remembering his own remaining share, O king, Sahadeva advanced on Shakuni in a gold-bodied chariot, stringing his strong bow and shaking the great bow.
Rushing at Subala's son, he struck him hard with vulture-feathered stone-whetted arrows, enraged, as one strikes a great elephant with goads.
The wise one said to him, holding him, as if reminding him: "Stand now in kshatriya duty and be a man; fight.
What you rejoiced in then, fool, playing with dice in the assembly—obtain the fruit of that deed today, ill-minded one.
Those evil-souled ones who laughed at us earlier are slain; Duryodhana, the burning brand of the family, and you, his maternal uncle, remain.
Today I shall strike off your head with a razor-arrow, like a fruit knocked from a tree with a heavy club."
Having said this, O great king, the mighty Sahadeva, tiger among men, enraged, advanced with speed.
Approaching, the unassailable Sahadeva, lord of warriors, drawing his strong bow, laughing in anger as it were,
pierced Shakuni with ten and his horses with four, cut his parasol, banner and bow, and roared like a lion.
With his banner, bow and parasol cut by Sahadeva, Subala's son was then pierced in all vital parts by many arrows.
Then again, O great king, the glorious Sahadeva sent at Shakuni an irresistible shower of arrows.
Then the son of Subala, enraged, wishing to kill Madri's son Sahadeva alone in the crush, swiftly leapt at him with a lance adorned with gold.
The son of Madri cut that raised lance and his well-rounded arms at the head of the battle with three broad-headed arrows at once, and roared loudly with force in the midst of the fight.
The quick-working one, with a well-aimed gold-feathered firm iron broad-headed arrow, piercing all coverings, again struck his head from his body.
With an arrow adorned with gold, bright as the sun, well whetted, the son of Subala, his head taken in the battle by the Pandava, fell to the ground.
The enraged son of Pandu covered that head with a swift, gold-feathered stone-whetted arrow—him who was the root of the Kurus' misconduct.
Seeing Shakuni lying on the ground with his head taken, limbs drenched in blood, your warriors, their courage lost to fear, fled in all directions with weapons in hand.
Fleeing, dry-mouthed, senseless, struck by Gandiva's roar and afflicted by fear, with broken chariots, horses and elephants and foot-soldiers, along with Dhritarashtra's men.
Then, having felled Shakuni from his chariot, the Pandavas, delighted, blew their conches in the battle, glad, with Keshava, gladdening their soldiers.
And all honouring Sahadeva, delighted, said to him in the battle: "By good fortune the deceitful, evil-souled one has been slain by you, hero, in the battle with his son."
Arjuna, firm for victory, received them, and the glorious Bhimasena, with the aspect of an enraged venomous serpent.
Dhananjaya with Gandiva made vain the resolve of the warriors with darts, rishtis and lances in hand, wishing to kill him.
Bibhatsu cut with broad-headed arrows the weapon-bearing arms of the rushing warriors, and their heads and horses.
Slain, they fell lifeless to the earth, struck quickly by Savyasachin, hero of the world.
Then King Duryodhana, seeing the destruction of his force, gathering the remnant, enraged, hundreds of chariots, lord,
elephants, horses and foot-soldiers, scorcher of foes, Dhritarashtra's son said these words to all assembled:
Meeting in the battle all the Pandavas with their friends, and the Panchala with his force, slay them quickly and return.
Taking his word on their heads, those arrogant in battle advanced on the Parthas by your son's command.
That force, O best of the Bharatas, in a moment was slain by the great souls in the battle and found no protector; standing armoured, it did not stand from fear.
With horses running about and the army covered with dust, in the battle neither quarters nor intermediate quarters could be made out.
Then many men issuing from the Pandava divisions struck yours in the battle, and in a moment, O Bharata, your force was left without a remnant.
Eleven akshauhinis of your son's, gathered, O Bharata, were slain in the battle by the Pandavas and Srinjayas, lord.
Of those thousands of kings, great souls, of yours, Duryodhana alone, O king, was seen, much wounded.
Then, looking in all directions, seeing the earth empty, bereft of all his warriors, and looking at the Pandavas in the battle,
glad, all their aims fulfilled, roaring on every side, and hearing the roar of arrows of those great souls,
Duryodhana, O great king, enveloped in stupor, bereft of force and mounts, set his mind on withdrawal.
[Dhritarashtra said:] "My army slain, the camp emptied, what force remained then of the Pandavas, charioteer? Tell me who ask, for you are skilled, Sanjaya.
And what did my foolish son Duryodhana do, seeing the destruction of his force, he alone, lord of the earth?"
[Sanjaya said:] "Two thousand chariots and seven hundred elephants, five thousand horses and a hundred hundred foot-soldiers—
this was the great force that remained of the Pandavas, O king, with which Dhrishtadyumna stood in the battle.
Alone, best of the Bharatas, King Duryodhana, best of chariot-warriors, then saw no ally in the battle.
Seeing the enemy roaring and the destruction of his own force, he abandoned his slain horse and fled in fear, turning away.
Your son Duryodhana, leader of eleven divisions, glorious, taking his mace, went on foot to a famous lake.
Going a short way on foot, the lord of men remembered the words of the wise, dharma-loving Kshatta (Vidura).
'Surely the greatly wise Vidura foresaw this long ago—the great destruction of us and of kshatriyas in battle.'
Thus reflecting, the king, wishing to enter the lake, his heart scorched with grief, seeing the destruction of his force,
and the Pandavas, O great king, led by Dhrishtadyumna, enraged, rushed at your force.
Dhananjaya with Gandiva made vain the resolve of the roaring warriors with darts, rishtis and lances in hand.
Having slain them with sharp arrows, with their ministers and kinsmen, Arjuna, standing on his white-horsed chariot, shone greatly.
With Subala's son slain along with his horses, chariots and elephants, your force was like a great forest cut down.
Of Duryodhana's force of many hundreds of thousands, no other great chariot-warrior was seen alive, O king,
except the hero Drona's son, Kritavarman, Kripa Gautama, O king, and your son the king.
Dhrishtadyumna, seeing me, said laughing to Satyaki: 'What use is it to hold him? He is of no use alive.'
Hearing Dhrishtadyumna's word, Shini's grandson, the great chariot-warrior, raised a sharp sword to kill me then.
Krishna Dvaipayana, the greatly wise, came to him and said: 'Release Sanjaya alive; he is not to be killed in any way.'
Hearing Dvaipayana's word, Shini's grandson with joined palms then said to me, releasing me: 'Go in peace, Sanjaya.'
Permitted by him, I, with my armour laid down and weaponless, set out for the city in the evening, drenched in blood.
A krosha away I saw Duryodhana standing alone, mace in hand, much wounded, O king.
With eyes full of tears he could not look at me; he looked sidelong, seeing me then standing wretched.
Seeing him too grieving alone in the battle, I could not say anything for a moment, steeped in sorrow.
Then I told him all about my capture and my release alive from the battle by Dvaipayana's grace.
After a moment's thought, regaining his senses, he asked me about his brothers and all the armies.
To him I told all as an eyewitness: that all his brothers were slain and the army felled.
'Three chariot-warriors, it is said, remain of yours, O king'—so Krishna Dvaipayana told me at my departure.
Sighing long, as it were, and looking at me again and again, your son, touching my shoulder with his hand, said:
'No one other than you, Sanjaya, is alive here in the battle; I see no second here, and the Pandavas have their allies.
Tell the king, Sanjaya, the lord whose eye is wisdom, that Duryodhana your son has entered a lake.
Bereft of such friends, sons and brothers, with the kingdom taken by the Pandavas, who like me would live?
Tell him all this: that I am freed from the great battle, sleeping in this lake of water, alive, greatly wounded.'
Having said this, O great king, the king entered that lake and by illusion made the water solid, the lord of men.
When he had entered the lake, I saw three chariots with tired horses coming together to that place:
Kripa Sharadvata the hero, Drona's son, best of chariot-warriors, and Bhoja Kritavarman, together and wounded by arrows.
All of them, seeing me, quickly urged their horses; coming up they said to me, 'By good fortune you live, Sanjaya.'
And all asked me, 'Is your son, King Duryodhana, alive, Sanjaya?'
I told them then that the king was safe and told them all that Duryodhana had said to me, and I told them of the lake which the lord of men had entered.
Ashvatthaman, hearing my words, O king, looking at that vast lake, lamented piteously:
'Alas! Fie! The lord of men does not know that we are alive! We together with him are enough to fight the enemy.'
Those great chariot-warriors, lamenting there a long time, fled, seeing the sons of Pandu in the battle.
Placing me on Kripa's well-appointed chariot, the three surviving chariot-warriors came to the camp.
There the troops, terrified, when the sun had set, all cried out on hearing of the destruction of your sons.
Then the aged men guarding the women, O great king, took the royal women and set out for the city.
There a great noise of wailing and weeping women everywhere arose, hearing of the destruction of the force.
Then those women, O king, crying again and again, made the earth resound with their cries like ospreys.
They struck their heads with nails and hands and tore their hair, crying out here and there.
Wailing "Alas", beating their breasts, they wept, lamenting, O lord of men.
Then Duryodhana's ministers, with tear-choked throats, greatly afflicted, took the royal women and set out for the city.
The gatekeepers, with canes and staves in hand, took costly couches with rich coverings and quickly went, guarding the women, to the city.
Others mounted chariots yoked with mules and, taking their own wives, went to the city.
The women, never before seen even by the sun in their houses, were seen by the people going to the city, O great king.
Those women, O best of the Bharatas, endowed with delicacy, went quickly to the city, their kinsmen and relatives slain.
From cowherds and shepherds on up, people ran to the city, bewildered, afflicted by fear of Bhimasena.
Great, most dreadful fear of the Parthas arose among them, and looking at one another they ran to the city.
While that dreadful flight went on, Yuyutsu, bewildered by grief, thought what was timely:
'Duryodhana is conquered in the battle by the Pandavas of terrible valour; the leader of eleven divisions and his brothers are slain, and all the Kurus led by Bhishma and Drona are slain.
I alone am freed, by fortune and chance; and all the camps on every side have fled.
Whatever of Duryodhana's ministers survive have taken the royal women and run to the city.
I think it time to enter with them, after obtaining the leave of Yudhishthira and Bhimasena.'
The mighty-armed one reported this matter to them both; the king, ever merciful, was pleased with him; embracing the vaishya woman's son, the mighty-armed one dismissed him.
Then he mounted a chariot and quickly urged the horses, and brought the royal women, though unhoped for, to the city.
With them he swiftly entered Hastinapura as the sun was setting, with throat choked by tears and eyes weeping.
He saw the greatly wise Vidura, his eyes full of tears, coming out from the king's presence, his mind struck by grief.
Vidura, firm in truth, said to him as he stood bowing before him: "In this Kuru destruction that has come to pass, by good fortune you live, son.
Without the king's entry why have you come here? Tell me all that cause in detail."
[Yuyutsu said:] "When Shakuni was slain, dear one, with his kin, sons and relatives, King Duryodhana, with the remnant of his retinue, abandoning his horse, fled in fear, turned away.
When the king had gone from the camp, everything, agitated with fear, fled to the city.
Then, placing the king's wives and his brothers' on mounts, the women's guards ran from fear.
Then I, with leave of the king along with Keshava, entered Hastinapura, to avoid the world's blame."
Hearing this said by the vaishya woman's son, Vidura, knower of all dharma, of immeasurable soul, knowing it timely, honoured Yuyutsu, who was skilled in speech.
All this is timely in the destruction of the Bharatas; today rest here, and tomorrow go to Yudhishthira.
Having said this, Vidura, knower of all dharma, dismissed Yuyutsu and entered the king's house; Yuyutsu too spent that night in his own house.
[Dhritarashtra said:] "Kritavarman, Kripa and valiant Drona's son, and Duryodhana, the dull-minded king—what did they do then?"
[Sanjaya said:] While the royal women were fleeing and the camp was empty, the three chariot-warriors were greatly agitated.
Hearing the sound of the victorious sons of Pandu, seeing the camp fled, in the evening, desiring the king, they did not like to stay there and went to the lake.
Yudhishthira too, the righteous, with his brothers, glad, rushed in the battle, O king, wishing to slay Duryodhana.
Searching for your son, enraged, eager for victory, striving and seeking, they did not see the lord of men.
With fierce speed, mace in hand, he had withdrawn and entered that lake, stopping the water by his illusion.
When all the Pandavas, their mounts quite exhausted, had reached their own camp, the soldiers halted.
Then Kripa, Drona's son and Kritavarman the Satvata, with the Parthas encamped, went slowly to that lake.
Reaching the lake where the king lay, they addressed the unassailable king, asleep in the water:

King, rise and fight Yudhishthira with us; either conquer and enjoy the earth, or slain, attain heaven.
mahabharata:9:29.12	Their whole force too has been slain by you, Duryodhana, and the soldiers who remain there are mostly stubborn.
mahabharata:9:29.13	They cannot bear your speed, O lord of men, protected by us; so rise, Bharata.
[Duryodhana said:] "By good fortune I see you freed from such a destruction of men, alive, bulls among men, from the Pandava-Kaurava crush.
We shall all conquer when rested and free of weariness; you are tired and I am much wounded; their strength is risen; therefore I do not choose to fight.
This is not wondrous, heroes, that your mind is great and your devotion to me supreme; but it is not the time for valour.
Resting one night today, together with you I shall fight the enemy; tomorrow I have no doubt in this."
[Sanjaya said:] Thus addressed, Drona's son said to the king, arrogant in battle: "Rise, king, good luck to you; we shall conquer the enemy in the battle.
By sacrifices and charity, by truth and by prayer, I swear, king, that today I shall slay the Somakas.
May I not attain the delight of sacrificers, fit for the good, if this night passing I do not slay the foes in the battle.
I shall not loose my armour without having slain all the Panchalas, lord; this I tell you truly; hear me, lord of men."
While they were speaking, hunters came to that place, weary with loads of meat, by chance for water.
Those hunters, O great king, always brought loads of meat to Bhimasena with the highest devotion, lord.
Standing there, they heard all that talk of theirs in secret and Duryodhana's words, meeting together.
Those mighty archers too, to the Kaurava who did not wish to fight, made a strong insistence, then, desiring battle.
Seeing them thus, the great chariot-warriors of the Kauravas and the king, unwilling to fight, standing in the water,
the hunters, hearing their conversation and the king standing in the water, recognised Suyodhana in the water.
They had earlier been asked by the son of Pandu about your son, and had come there by chance, searching for the king.
Then, remembering the Pandava's words, O king, the deer-hunters said slowly to one another:

Let us make Duryodhana known; the Pandava will give us wealth; it is clear that King Duryodhana is known to us to be in the lake.
mahabharata:9:29.31	Therefore let us all go to where King Yudhishthira is, to tell that the impatient Duryodhana lies asleep in the water.
mahabharata:9:29.32	We shall all tell the wise Bhimasena, the bearer of a bow, that Dhritarashtra's son lies in the water.
mahabharata:9:29.33	He will give us, well pleased, much wealth; what use to us is dry, trouble-giving meat that withers?
Having said this, the hunters, delighted, desiring wealth, took their loads of meat and set out for the camp.
The Pandavas, O great king, having attained their aims, strikers, not seeing Duryodhana standing in the battle,
wishing to reach the end of the deceitful sinner, sent spies on every side to that battlefield.
Coming back, the soldiers of the king of dharma reported together that King Duryodhana was lost.
Hearing that report of the spies, O best of the Bharatas, the king fell into deep thought and sighed.
Then, as the distressed Pandavas, O best of the Bharatas, were standing, the hunters, hastening, left that place,
and came to the camp, glad, having seen King Duryodhana; held back, they entered in the sight of Bhimasena.
Reaching the Pandava, mighty Bhimasena, they told him all that had happened and been heard.
Then Vrikodara, O king, giving them much wealth, scorcher of foes, told it all to the king of dharma.
This Duryodhana, O king, has been found by my hunters; stopping the water, he lies for whose sake you suffer.
Hearing those pleasing words of Bhimasena, O lord of men, the unconquered son of Kunti was glad with his brothers.
Hearing that the mighty archer had entered the water lake, he quickly went there, putting Janardana before him.
Then a clamour arose, O lord of men, of the delighted Pandavas and all the Panchalas.
They raised lion-roars and shouts, O best of the Bharatas; swiftly the kshatriyas, O king, went to the Dvaipayana lake.
The sinful son of Dhritarashtra is found and seen!—so the Somakas cried out repeatedly there, delighted on all sides.
A tumultuous noise of those quickly going chariots touched heaven, O lord of the earth.
Wishing to save Duryodhana, here and there, they followed Yudhishthira, quickly, the king, their mounts tired.
Arjuna, Bhimasena, the two sons of Madri, Dhrishtadyumna the Panchala, and the unconquered Shikhandin,
Uttamaujas, Yudhamanyu and the unconquered Satyaki, and the remaining Panchalas and the sons of Draupadi, O Bharata, all horses and elephants and hundreds of foot-soldiers,
thus the king of dharma Yudhishthira, O great king, came to the famed Dvaipayana lake where Duryodhana was.
Cool, spotless, charming water, like a second ocean, where your son stood, having stopped the water by illusion.
There thousands of crows spent that night, sleeping happily, O Kaurava, each in its own refuge.
That your face is wet with fallen tears, O king, is not seen in the scriptures; the wise do not praise it.
Having said so, Pritha dismissed him and went home. That hero was slain by Arjuna, brother by brother, uterine kin.
[The serpent said:] "All these are not independent, like the rod, wheel and so on; so am I also; therefore I do not consider myself the cause for you."
Your mind is not made up, dear one; again you are bewildered by childishness; why do we all lament in the air again and again?
And Gandhari too, with various funeral rites for her sons, came to freedom from the debt, giving desired things to Brahmanas.
The Vrishnis felt no shame in doing sinful deeds then; they hated Brahmanas, fathers and gods too.
I am Agni, best of the Kurus; Khandava was burned by me, by Arjuna's power and Narayana's.
I wish to see that Panchali too, who followed dharma; and I do not wish to stay here; this I tell you truly.
